# Buying Imported Foods and Homeware in Mexico

Learn about stores and emporiums where you can buy imported foods and goods which years ago were not available anywhere in Mexico

 by [Mexperience](https://www.mexperience.com/author/Mexperience/ "All posts by Mexperience")

[![Image 14: Fine wine and glasses](https://www.mexperience.com/wp-content/uploads/Wine-and-Glasses-NBS-750x375.jpg)](https://www.mexperience.com/buying-imported-foods-and-homeware-in-mexico/ "Permalink to Buying Imported Foods and Homeware in Mexico")

When Mexico began to open its markets in the 1980s, it became easier to buy certain foods and homeware items that before then weren’t available at all. Today, the retail landscapes in Mexico include US-style supermarkets, hypermarkets, membership discount emporiums, modern department stores, and a range of specialized retail outlets which cater to ‘foodies’ and the well heeled.

## Product availability can vary

One of the quirky features of the Mexican retail space is the [inconsistent availability](https://www.mexperience.com/no-hay/) of certain products, and this especially pertinent to imported food and drinks.

You might wander along the aisles of your local supermarket or membership store one day and discover, for the first time, a brand or product you enjoyed back home. You might also grimace at the price tag, and buy it anyway. When you go back to buy it again next month, it’s not there—and later realize that it never returns.

This ‘batch availability’ of imported foods is surprisingly common in Mexico, which is why seasoned foreign residents might purchase more than one in expectation of it not being available again—and consider the item as a treat. This can apply to anything: your favorite brand of peanut butter, a certain variety of chocolate bar, a gourmet food ingredient, and especially [varieties of teas](https://www.mexperience.com/searching-for-camellia-sinensis/).

## Specialist food and homeware stores in Mexico

Here is a list of stores in Mexico where you are most likely to find those goods and goodies you enjoyed buying in the USA, Canada, or Europe and of the kind you certainly won’t find at your [local tiendita](https://www.mexperience.com/just-for-your-convenience/).

### La Comer and Fresko

When Commercial Mexicana sold-off its supermarket chain to Soriana, it kept some of the larger stores and re-branded them to “[La Comer.](http://www.lacomer.com.mx/tienda/)” These larger ‘hypermarkets’ offer food, drink, and a range of homeware products under one roof. The grocery aisles feature a ‘gourmet and imported goods’ section which displays an array of fancy and specialist foods and drinks—a ‘lite’ version of its City Market outlets, see below. La Comer has a sister-store named [Fresko](https://www.lacomer.com.mx/) that offers virtually the same lines of products as La Comer in smaller stores and with a particular focus on fresh produce.

### City Market

Owned by La Comer, [City Market](http://www.citymarket.com.mx/) is a chic and up-scale gourmet purveyor of all things _foodie_ and _homestyle_ and is Mexico’s answer to Whole Foods in the US, or Waitrose in the UK. City Market stores also feature a café, a fresh sushi bar, and a [gourmet ice-cream](https://www.mexperience.com/a-scoop-on-mexican-ice-cream/) parlor.

Their stores are situated in Mexico City’s more exclusive neighborhoods and the company is gradually expanding this retail format into the provinces. Outside of the capital there are City Market stores located in Querétaro, Metepec, Cuernavaca, Guadalajara, San Miguel de Allende, and Monterrey.

In addition to the extensive ranges of gourmet and exotic foods available here, City Market also offers a ‘Spa’ section which further entices shoppers with fine soaps, bath salts and towels, as well as a range of aromatherapy products.

This is not somewhere you go looking for bargains, although the stocked ranges of specialist and imported foods and food ingredients as well as its selection of fine wines and imported liquors is substantial.

### La Europea

As the name suggests, [La Europea](http://www.laeuropea.com.mx/) is a specialist purveyor of imported goods offers a comprehensive choice of imported wines, liquors, and gourmet food products.

Established since 1957, the chain has moved with the times to offer an expanding range of products across its stores. La Europea has branches in many key cities across Mexico, and while you’ll often find things here not available elsewhere (except perhaps at the few branches of City Market), like City Market, it’s best not to cavil about the prices.

### Williams Sonoma

If you enjoy home cooking and all things kitchen, you’ll be pleased to learn that Williams-Sonoma, the American purveyor of high-end kitchen tools and cookware popular in the US, has opened stores in Mexico.

They offer in-store and online shopping, with free delivery and returns within 30 days. Their price tags are generally high, although they often run discount sales, some of which are significant and make their prices competitive with other online sellers. This store is ideal when you’re looking for a special gift, or ranges of specialized kitchenware of the kind you’re unlikely to find in other department stores.

### HEB Mexico

The Texas-based [HEB superstore](http://www.heb.com.mx/) stocks an ample range of American goods. HEB Mexico stores are principally based in the country’s north-eastern states, as well as Guanajuato and Aguascalientes, although they continue to expand and, if there’s an HEB locally where you live, you will be able to find an extensive range of imported food and homeware products here, including well-stocked fresh produce sections.

### CostCo and Sam’s Club

[CostCo](http://www.costco.com.mx/) and [Sam’s Club](https://www.sams.com.mx/) are “Members Only” emporiums that require you to purchase an annual membership to spend your money at them. However, they do offer a wide choice of imported foods, drinks, and homeware goods, and through direct discounts or points that you accumulate as you buy (and later trade for other goods in-store), your annual membership may be returned when your shop here. Many foreign residents hold membership cards to one or both stores which are situated in towns and cities across Mexico.

### The Home Store

A specialist homeware and lifestyle department store with branches in Mexico City as well as some of Mexico’s larger cities, [The Home Store](http://www.thehomestore.com.mx/) offers an impressive range of homeware items across various departments including bedroom, kitchen, dining room, and utility areas; it also offers ranges of complementary homeware products like interior décor, wellness, and home-style accessories.

### Pottery Barn

This San Francisco-based upscale home furnishing and lifestyle accessories store has been operating in Mexico for a few years, with shops situated in some of Mexico City’s chic malls as well as a store operating in the city of León in the state of Guanajuato.[Pottery Barn](https://www.potterybarn.com.mx/) also has sister stores in Mexico which stock its archetypal furnishings and accessories aimed at [kids](https://www.potterybarnkids.com.mx/) and [teens](https://www.pbteen.com.mx/).

### The ‘big three’ department stores

[Liverpool](https://www.liverpool.com.mx/), [Palacio de Hierro](https://www.elpalaciodehierro.com/), and [Sears](https://www.sears.com.mx/)—Mexico’s three biggest department stores are also among Mexico’s biggest importers, and foreign residents often repair to one of these establishments to find products they want or need which they cannot find elsewhere. These department stores stock imported brands of fine foods, considerable ranges of homewares and furnishings, a wide assortment of domestic appliances, and clothes among many other things—and local prices vary from reasonable to cheeky in relation to prices for the same products sold in the USA.

### Amazon Mexico

Products you seek might be available through [Amazon Mexico](https://www.amazon.com.mx/). Not everything that’s available in the USA, for example, will be available through Amazon Mexico, but the company is expanding its Mexican operations appreciably to offer ever-wider ranges of imported products on offer direct from Amazon’s warehouses in Mexico.

Items available only from Amazon abroad might not ship to Mexico and where they do, delivered prices are likely to be higher in part due to import duties, Mexico’s [sales tax rate](https://www.mexperience.com/lifestyle/mexico-essentials/mexico-in-facts-figures/#IVA), and shipping costs—all of which add to the price of any items you order online which are delivered from outside Mexico.

If you subscribe to Amazon’s Mexico Prime Membership plan, you can obtain free delivery on a range of products (not all) shipped from Mexico as well as some shipped from the USA. (If you have an Amazon Prime subscription from overseas, it does _not_ qualify you for free shipping to/in Mexico; you have to buy an Amazon Prime Mexico subscription.)

## The cost of living in Mexico

The Mexperience [Mexico Cost of Living Guide](https://www.mexperience.com/lifestyle/living-in-mexico/cost-of-living-in-mexico/) offers a comprehensive resource to help you to create a detailed budget for your finances in Mexico, based on your individual circumstances and lifestyle plans.

# Buying Imported Foods and Homeware in Mexico

Learn about stores and emporiums where you can buy imported foods and goods which years ago were not available anywhere in Mexico

 by [Mexperience](https://www.mexperience.com/author/Mexperience/ "All posts by Mexperience")

[![Image 14: Fine wine and glasses](https://www.mexperience.com/wp-content/uploads/Wine-and-Glasses-NBS-750x375.jpg)](https://www.mexperience.com/buying-imported-foods-and-homeware-in-mexico/ "Permalink to Buying Imported Foods and Homeware in Mexico")

When Mexico began to open its markets in the 1980s, it became easier to buy certain foods and homeware items that before then weren’t available at all. Today, the retail landscapes in Mexico include US-style supermarkets, hypermarkets, membership discount emporiums, modern department stores, and a range of specialized retail outlets which cater to ‘foodies’ and the well heeled.

## Product availability can vary

One of the quirky features of the Mexican retail space is the [inconsistent availability](https://www.mexperience.com/no-hay/) of certain products, and this especially pertinent to imported food and drinks.

You might wander along the aisles of your local supermarket or membership store one day and discover, for the first time, a brand or product you enjoyed back home. You might also grimace at the price tag, and buy it anyway. When you go back to buy it again next month, it’s not there—and later realize that it never returns.

This ‘batch availability’ of imported foods is surprisingly common in Mexico, which is why seasoned foreign residents might purchase more than one in expectation of it not being available again—and consider the item as a treat. This can apply to anything: your favorite brand of peanut butter, a certain variety of chocolate bar, a gourmet food ingredient, and especially [varieties of teas](https://www.mexperience.com/searching-for-camellia-sinensis/).

## Specialist food and homeware stores in Mexico

Here is a list of stores in Mexico where you are most likely to find those goods and goodies you enjoyed buying in the USA, Canada, or Europe and of the kind you certainly won’t find at your [local tiendita](https://www.mexperience.com/just-for-your-convenience/).

### La Comer and Fresko

When Commercial Mexicana sold-off its supermarket chain to Soriana, it kept some of the larger stores and re-branded them to “[La Comer.](http://www.lacomer.com.mx/tienda/)” These larger ‘hypermarkets’ offer food, drink, and a range of homeware products under one roof. The grocery aisles feature a ‘gourmet and imported goods’ section which displays an array of fancy and specialist foods and drinks—a ‘lite’ version of its City Market outlets, see below. La Comer has a sister-store named [Fresko](https://www.lacomer.com.mx/) that offers virtually the same lines of products as La Comer in smaller stores and with a particular focus on fresh produce.

### City Market

Owned by La Comer, [City Market](http://www.citymarket.com.mx/) is a chic and up-scale gourmet purveyor of all things _foodie_ and _homestyle_ and is Mexico’s answer to Whole Foods in the US, or Waitrose in the UK. City Market stores also feature a café, a fresh sushi bar, and a [gourmet ice-cream](https://www.mexperience.com/a-scoop-on-mexican-ice-cream/) parlor.

Their stores are situated in Mexico City’s more exclusive neighborhoods and the company is gradually expanding this retail format into the provinces. Outside of the capital there are City Market stores located in Querétaro, Metepec, Cuernavaca, Guadalajara, San Miguel de Allende, and Monterrey.

In addition to the extensive ranges of gourmet and exotic foods available here, City Market also offers a ‘Spa’ section which further entices shoppers with fine soaps, bath salts and towels, as well as a range of aromatherapy products.

This is not somewhere you go looking for bargains, although the stocked ranges of specialist and imported foods and food ingredients as well as its selection of fine wines and imported liquors is substantial.

### La Europea

As the name suggests, [La Europea](http://www.laeuropea.com.mx/) is a specialist purveyor of imported goods offers a comprehensive choice of imported wines, liquors, and gourmet food products.

Established since 1957, the chain has moved with the times to offer an expanding range of products across its stores. La Europea has branches in many key cities across Mexico, and while you’ll often find things here not available elsewhere (except perhaps at the few branches of City Market), like City Market, it’s best not to cavil about the prices.

### Williams Sonoma

If you enjoy home cooking and all things kitchen, you’ll be pleased to learn that Williams-Sonoma, the American purveyor of high-end kitchen tools and cookware popular in the US, has opened stores in Mexico.

They offer in-store and online shopping, with free delivery and returns within 30 days. Their price tags are generally high, although they often run discount sales, some of which are significant and make their prices competitive with other online sellers. This store is ideal when you’re looking for a special gift, or ranges of specialized kitchenware of the kind you’re unlikely to find in other department stores.

### HEB Mexico

The Texas-based [HEB superstore](http://www.heb.com.mx/) stocks an ample range of American goods. HEB Mexico stores are principally based in the country’s north-eastern states, as well as Guanajuato and Aguascalientes, although they continue to expand and, if there’s an HEB locally where you live, you will be able to find an extensive range of imported food and homeware products here, including well-stocked fresh produce sections.

### CostCo and Sam’s Club

[CostCo](http://www.costco.com.mx/) and [Sam’s Club](https://www.sams.com.mx/) are “Members Only” emporiums that require you to purchase an annual membership to spend your money at them. However, they do offer a wide choice of imported foods, drinks, and homeware goods, and through direct discounts or points that you accumulate as you buy (and later trade for other goods in-store), your annual membership may be returned when your shop here. Many foreign residents hold membership cards to one or both stores which are situated in towns and cities across Mexico.

### The Home Store

A specialist homeware and lifestyle department store with branches in Mexico City as well as some of Mexico’s larger cities, [The Home Store](http://www.thehomestore.com.mx/) offers an impressive range of homeware items across various departments including bedroom, kitchen, dining room, and utility areas; it also offers ranges of complementary homeware products like interior décor, wellness, and home-style accessories.

### Pottery Barn

This San Francisco-based upscale home furnishing and lifestyle accessories store has been operating in Mexico for a few years, with shops situated in some of Mexico City’s chic malls as well as a store operating in the city of León in the state of Guanajuato.[Pottery Barn](https://www.potterybarn.com.mx/) also has sister stores in Mexico which stock its archetypal furnishings and accessories aimed at [kids](https://www.potterybarnkids.com.mx/) and [teens](https://www.pbteen.com.mx/).

### The ‘big three’ department stores

[Liverpool](https://www.liverpool.com.mx/), [Palacio de Hierro](https://www.elpalaciodehierro.com/), and [Sears](https://www.sears.com.mx/)—Mexico’s three biggest department stores are also among Mexico’s biggest importers, and foreign residents often repair to one of these establishments to find products they want or need which they cannot find elsewhere. These department stores stock imported brands of fine foods, considerable ranges of homewares and furnishings, a wide assortment of domestic appliances, and clothes among many other things—and local prices vary from reasonable to cheeky in relation to prices for the same products sold in the USA.

### Amazon Mexico

Products you seek might be available through [Amazon Mexico](https://www.amazon.com.mx/). Not everything that’s available in the USA, for example, will be available through Amazon Mexico, but the company is expanding its Mexican operations appreciably to offer ever-wider ranges of imported products on offer direct from Amazon’s warehouses in Mexico.

Items available only from Amazon abroad might not ship to Mexico and where they do, delivered prices are likely to be higher in part due to import duties, Mexico’s [sales tax rate](https://www.mexperience.com/lifestyle/mexico-essentials/mexico-in-facts-figures/#IVA), and shipping costs—all of which add to the price of any items you order online which are delivered from outside Mexico.

If you subscribe to Amazon’s Mexico Prime Membership plan, you can obtain free delivery on a range of products (not all) shipped from Mexico as well as some shipped from the USA. (If you have an Amazon Prime subscription from overseas, it does _not_ qualify you for free shipping to/in Mexico; you have to buy an Amazon Prime Mexico subscription.)

## The cost of living in Mexico

The Mexperience [Mexico Cost of Living Guide](https://www.mexperience.com/lifestyle/living-in-mexico/cost-of-living-in-mexico/) offers a comprehensive resource to help you to create a detailed budget for your finances in Mexico, based on your individual circumstances and lifestyle plans.

# Mexico City’s Markets

[](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/author/admin/)

[Anais Martinez](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/author/admin/)

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fmexico-citys-markets%2F)[](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fmexico-citys-markets%2F&media=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2025%2F04%2F045A0051-770x1155.jpg&description=Mexico%20City%26%238217%3Bs%20Markets)[](whatsapp://send?text=Mexico%20City%E2%80%99s%20Markets%20%E2%80%93%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fmexico-citys-markets%2F)

I really think the easiest and fastest way to get heart of a culture, their traditions and every day life is stepping into their markets. Mexico is not the exception, in fact, even in a sprawling metropolis like Mexico City, markets are still one of the most unique reflections of our daily life.

Markets have been central to Mexican culture since long before the Spanish arrived. Back then, they were known as _tiānquiz(tli)_, a Nahuatl word that eventually evolved into _tianguis_, still used today to describe informal, pop-up street markets.

These venues weren’t just where trade happened. They were lively hubs where producers, farmers, and travelers exchanged goods, stories, and sometimes even languages. The market was (and still is) a living social network, completely tied to our identity.

Today, Mexico City is home to a wide variety of markets, each serving a specific purpose depending sometimes on the neighborhood and others on the ingredients you’re looking for. I can be confusing at times but here’s a quick breakdown.

## Types of Markets in Mexico City

## **Mercados.**

Permanent, often government-regulated markets housed in buildings of brick and mortar.

These are spaces with assigned stalls, that may as well be considered as a “one stop shop” offering everything from meat & poultry, to spice and chile vendors, juice stands, to food courts, flowers, plants and sometimes even witchcraft mixed with medicinal teas and herbs.

There are more than 300 public markets across Mexico City, basically one in every neighborhood. They vary dramatically in size, from tiny 10×10 meter corners to entire city blocks that sometimes even end up merging into the nearby streets creating entire zones dedicated to commerce, like we see around Merced Market.

Most markets are open between 9am and 5pm , with very few exceptions, and some vendors might take Sunday off, which makes it easier for housewives and homemakers timings, but a bit harder for people who work standard office hours.

## Tianguis.

These temporary markets pop up on specific days of the week, often taking over a few blocks of a street. They’re perfect for scoring seasonal produce, street food, and the occasional unexpected gem.

Because they’re only around for a few hours, neighbors look forward to the day their local tianguis appears; it’s a chance to get fresh ingredients without commuting far. It’s also where you can build a real connection with your vendor. Ask for “one avocado for today and another for the weekend,” and you’ll walk away with two perfectly chosen specimens.

Set-up usually begins around 7 AM, with each vendor arriving and quickly building their stall from metal tubes and colorful tarps. By 6 PM, it’s as if nothing ever happened—the street returns to its everyday self, like magic

## Here’s a quick guide of some of the main tianguis & mercados in Mexico City.

Be sure to carry cash with you when visiting as credit cards are mostly not accepted, and keep in mind we don’t tend to haggle but sometime you might get a little extra apple or flower from the vendors.

## Mercado Medellín

Its location in the heart of Roma along with its manageable size, makes this market a perfect option for solo travelers. Aside from the usual sections, here you’ll find some stalls selling South American ingredientes and produce which cannot be found elsewhere.

**On weekends, don’t miss the butcher at the very end of the meat section, he serves up some of the best carnitas tacos around. Totally worth a stop.**

## Mercado Jamaica

This isn’t just one of my favorite markets in the city, it’s also home to the largest flower market in the country, located right behind the main building.

What sets it apart from other markets is its layout: two very different buildings. One dates back to the late 1950s and follows the classic market format, with all the usual sections. The newer, much larger building, is something else completely. It’s where over 5,000 varieties of flowers are sold daily, and it also serves as a central hub for one of Mexico’s most iconic celebrations: **Día de Muertos.**

As the holiday approaches, flower trucks arrive from the farms packed to the brim with blooms. Marigolds ( which are indigenous to Mexico, by the way) are tightly stacked in the backs of trucks, their scent blending beautifully with the nearby vendors selling copal and incense.

And don’t worry if you can’t make it during this magical season. This market is also home to some of my absolute favorite bites in Mexico City. They’re so good, I’ve brought TV crews and chefs from around the world to try them. ([Read more about who, here)](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/about/press_and_media/).

**You can join too, just sign up for my “[Good Morning CDMX](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/foodtours/good-morning-cdmx/)” tour and I’ll happily show you around.**

## Mercado San Juan

This is what I like to call our “gourmet market” one of the most well-known and tourist-friendly spots in the city. Think of it as Mexico’s version of Whole Foods. It may not look fancy at first but if you know what to look for, you’ll spot some truly exceptional finds.

You’ll come across top-quality fish you won’t find anywhere else in the city, along with meats like rabbit, crocodile, venison, ostrich, and baby goat (just a heads-up, you might catch them skinning it right on the spot). And for the more adventurous eaters, there’s a whole selection of edible insects: agave worms, ant larvae, and my personal favorite—crispy, delicious grasshoppers.

**.Get some fresh fruit from the stand El Paraíso and enjoy the coffee and incredible hospitality by Pablo at Triana Cafe.**

![Image 4](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/marigold2-768x1024.jpg)

## Central de Abastos

Central de Abastos isn’t just Mexico City’s largest market, it’s the largest wholesale market in the whole world. Spanning approximately 327 hectares (about 808 acres) in the Iztapalapa district, this enormous hub moves over 30,000 tons of goods every day and sees more than 300,000 visitors daily.

It’s like a city within a city, complete with its own police force, multiple banks, rest areas for drivers, and even daycare services for working mothers. There’s even a toll at the entrance, with pricing based on the size of your vehicle.

Virtually everything sold in Mexico City passes through this market at some point, making it a key player in the country’s food system. It’s even considered the second most economically active place in Mexico, right after the stock market. And despite its scale, the market still runs mostly on cash, giving it a raw, authentic energy that’s rare to find at this scale.

**If you can find the Tortas de la basura please stand in line to get them they are the tastiest bite. And if too overwhelmed to go on your own, I’d be happy to take you around.**

![Image 6](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/central-de-abastos.jpg)

## Mercado Merced

La Merced, as it’s known, is a sprawling complex made up of several sections, including the Nave Mayor, Nave Menor, the candy aisle, Banquetón, Merced 2000, and the area known as Los Fierros. Its easy access via the subway makes it a go-to spot for chefs and restaurants sourcing fresh, specialty ingredients daily.

That said, the surrounding neighborhood is known for daytime prostitutions and petty crime, (pickpocketing and scams are definitely not uncommon) so it’s important to stay aware if you’re exploring solo.

**If you manage to find your way to the Banquetón section, do yourself a favor and track down the McTeo taco stand. Their carne enchilada tacos served with French fries and grilles spring onions? Absolute magic**

![Image 8](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Tacos_McTeo-1024x681.jpg)

## Tianguis de la Lagunilla

One of the largest and most iconic _tianguis_ in the city sets up every Sunday at the intersection of three otherwise ordinary streets.

By 10 AM, vendors are fully set up, offering everything from 1960s memorabilia, vinyl records, and vintage movie posters to fur coats, mid-century furniture and an almost absurd number of antique door knobs (for some reason still unknown to me).

And of course, no _tianguis_ in Mexico would be complete without its fair share of street food. This one is packed with hidden gems, but the real must is grabbing a michelada served in a one-liter cup, rimmed with tamarind paste and candied sesame seeds. Trust me, it’s non-negotiable.

**If you are a savvy tianguis connoisseur find the bacalao tortas. If not, come with me on the [Sunday at Lagunilla Tour](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/foodtours/lagunilla/).**

## Tianguis de la Condesa

Want to experience everyday life at a local tianguis? Head to Campeche Street in Condesa every Friday. You’ll find everything from gardening tools and clothing to cheese, chicken vendors, perfectly ripe fruits, fresh-cut flowers, and lush plants. And of course, food stalls are scattered all along the way.

**Be sure to stop by the quesadilla stand for fresh masa delights, especially the tlacoyos stuffed with fava beans and their blue corn gorditas stuffed with chicharron, simple, satisfying, and full of flavor**

## Mercado el Cien

Even though it’s technically a pop-up market, this one is referred to as a mercado, and for good reason. It was the first major farmer’s market in Mexico City and has since become a go-to spot for locals and chefs searching for the freshest organic produce.

Its name comes from the concept that everything sold here is grown, raised, or produced within a 100-mile radius. That may not always hold true today, but it’s still one of the best places to connect directly with the people growing your food.

Showing up in your hippest outfit and carrying your trendiest tote isn’t required, but it’s definitely encouraged.

**This is also where I discovered (and instantly fell in love with) Simbiotica kombucha, so make sure to grab a bottle while you’re there.**

![Image 10](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Mercado_el_cien_2-1024x768.jpg)

# Mexico City’s Markets

[](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/author/admin/)

[Anais Martinez](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/author/admin/)

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fmexico-citys-markets%2F)[](https://www.pinterest.com/pin/create/button/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fmexico-citys-markets%2F&media=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fwp-content%2Fuploads%2F2025%2F04%2F045A0051-770x1155.jpg&description=Mexico%20City%26%238217%3Bs%20Markets)[](whatsapp://send?text=Mexico%20City%E2%80%99s%20Markets%20%E2%80%93%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.thecuriousmexican.com%2Fmexico-citys-markets%2F)

I really think the easiest and fastest way to get heart of a culture, their traditions and every day life is stepping into their markets. Mexico is not the exception, in fact, even in a sprawling metropolis like Mexico City, markets are still one of the most unique reflections of our daily life.

Markets have been central to Mexican culture since long before the Spanish arrived. Back then, they were known as _tiānquiz(tli)_, a Nahuatl word that eventually evolved into _tianguis_, still used today to describe informal, pop-up street markets.

These venues weren’t just where trade happened. They were lively hubs where producers, farmers, and travelers exchanged goods, stories, and sometimes even languages. The market was (and still is) a living social network, completely tied to our identity.

Today, Mexico City is home to a wide variety of markets, each serving a specific purpose depending sometimes on the neighborhood and others on the ingredients you’re looking for. I can be confusing at times but here’s a quick breakdown.

## Types of Markets in Mexico City

## **Mercados.**

Permanent, often government-regulated markets housed in buildings of brick and mortar.

These are spaces with assigned stalls, that may as well be considered as a “one stop shop” offering everything from meat & poultry, to spice and chile vendors, juice stands, to food courts, flowers, plants and sometimes even witchcraft mixed with medicinal teas and herbs.

There are more than 300 public markets across Mexico City, basically one in every neighborhood. They vary dramatically in size, from tiny 10×10 meter corners to entire city blocks that sometimes even end up merging into the nearby streets creating entire zones dedicated to commerce, like we see around Merced Market.

Most markets are open between 9am and 5pm , with very few exceptions, and some vendors might take Sunday off, which makes it easier for housewives and homemakers timings, but a bit harder for people who work standard office hours.

## Tianguis.

These temporary markets pop up on specific days of the week, often taking over a few blocks of a street. They’re perfect for scoring seasonal produce, street food, and the occasional unexpected gem.

Because they’re only around for a few hours, neighbors look forward to the day their local tianguis appears; it’s a chance to get fresh ingredients without commuting far. It’s also where you can build a real connection with your vendor. Ask for “one avocado for today and another for the weekend,” and you’ll walk away with two perfectly chosen specimens.

Set-up usually begins around 7 AM, with each vendor arriving and quickly building their stall from metal tubes and colorful tarps. By 6 PM, it’s as if nothing ever happened—the street returns to its everyday self, like magic

## Here’s a quick guide of some of the main tianguis & mercados in Mexico City.

Be sure to carry cash with you when visiting as credit cards are mostly not accepted, and keep in mind we don’t tend to haggle but sometime you might get a little extra apple or flower from the vendors.

## Mercado Medellín

Its location in the heart of Roma along with its manageable size, makes this market a perfect option for solo travelers. Aside from the usual sections, here you’ll find some stalls selling South American ingredientes and produce which cannot be found elsewhere.

**On weekends, don’t miss the butcher at the very end of the meat section, he serves up some of the best carnitas tacos around. Totally worth a stop.**

## Mercado Jamaica

This isn’t just one of my favorite markets in the city, it’s also home to the largest flower market in the country, located right behind the main building.

What sets it apart from other markets is its layout: two very different buildings. One dates back to the late 1950s and follows the classic market format, with all the usual sections. The newer, much larger building, is something else completely. It’s where over 5,000 varieties of flowers are sold daily, and it also serves as a central hub for one of Mexico’s most iconic celebrations: **Día de Muertos.**

As the holiday approaches, flower trucks arrive from the farms packed to the brim with blooms. Marigolds ( which are indigenous to Mexico, by the way) are tightly stacked in the backs of trucks, their scent blending beautifully with the nearby vendors selling copal and incense.

And don’t worry if you can’t make it during this magical season. This market is also home to some of my absolute favorite bites in Mexico City. They’re so good, I’ve brought TV crews and chefs from around the world to try them. ([Read more about who, here)](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/about/press_and_media/).

**You can join too, just sign up for my “[Good Morning CDMX](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/foodtours/good-morning-cdmx/)” tour and I’ll happily show you around.**

## Mercado San Juan

This is what I like to call our “gourmet market” one of the most well-known and tourist-friendly spots in the city. Think of it as Mexico’s version of Whole Foods. It may not look fancy at first but if you know what to look for, you’ll spot some truly exceptional finds.

You’ll come across top-quality fish you won’t find anywhere else in the city, along with meats like rabbit, crocodile, venison, ostrich, and baby goat (just a heads-up, you might catch them skinning it right on the spot). And for the more adventurous eaters, there’s a whole selection of edible insects: agave worms, ant larvae, and my personal favorite—crispy, delicious grasshoppers.

**.Get some fresh fruit from the stand El Paraíso and enjoy the coffee and incredible hospitality by Pablo at Triana Cafe.**

![Image 4](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/marigold2-768x1024.jpg)

## Central de Abastos

Central de Abastos isn’t just Mexico City’s largest market, it’s the largest wholesale market in the whole world. Spanning approximately 327 hectares (about 808 acres) in the Iztapalapa district, this enormous hub moves over 30,000 tons of goods every day and sees more than 300,000 visitors daily.

It’s like a city within a city, complete with its own police force, multiple banks, rest areas for drivers, and even daycare services for working mothers. There’s even a toll at the entrance, with pricing based on the size of your vehicle.

Virtually everything sold in Mexico City passes through this market at some point, making it a key player in the country’s food system. It’s even considered the second most economically active place in Mexico, right after the stock market. And despite its scale, the market still runs mostly on cash, giving it a raw, authentic energy that’s rare to find at this scale.

**If you can find the Tortas de la basura please stand in line to get them they are the tastiest bite. And if too overwhelmed to go on your own, I’d be happy to take you around.**

![Image 6](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/central-de-abastos.jpg)

## Mercado Merced

La Merced, as it’s known, is a sprawling complex made up of several sections, including the Nave Mayor, Nave Menor, the candy aisle, Banquetón, Merced 2000, and the area known as Los Fierros. Its easy access via the subway makes it a go-to spot for chefs and restaurants sourcing fresh, specialty ingredients daily.

That said, the surrounding neighborhood is known for daytime prostitutions and petty crime, (pickpocketing and scams are definitely not uncommon) so it’s important to stay aware if you’re exploring solo.

**If you manage to find your way to the Banquetón section, do yourself a favor and track down the McTeo taco stand. Their carne enchilada tacos served with French fries and grilles spring onions? Absolute magic**

![Image 8](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Tacos_McTeo-1024x681.jpg)

## Tianguis de la Lagunilla

One of the largest and most iconic _tianguis_ in the city sets up every Sunday at the intersection of three otherwise ordinary streets.

By 10 AM, vendors are fully set up, offering everything from 1960s memorabilia, vinyl records, and vintage movie posters to fur coats, mid-century furniture and an almost absurd number of antique door knobs (for some reason still unknown to me).

And of course, no _tianguis_ in Mexico would be complete without its fair share of street food. This one is packed with hidden gems, but the real must is grabbing a michelada served in a one-liter cup, rimmed with tamarind paste and candied sesame seeds. Trust me, it’s non-negotiable.

**If you are a savvy tianguis connoisseur find the bacalao tortas. If not, come with me on the [Sunday at Lagunilla Tour](https://www.thecuriousmexican.com/foodtours/lagunilla/).**

## Tianguis de la Condesa

Want to experience everyday life at a local tianguis? Head to Campeche Street in Condesa every Friday. You’ll find everything from gardening tools and clothing to cheese, chicken vendors, perfectly ripe fruits, fresh-cut flowers, and lush plants. And of course, food stalls are scattered all along the way.

**Be sure to stop by the quesadilla stand for fresh masa delights, especially the tlacoyos stuffed with fava beans and their blue corn gorditas stuffed with chicharron, simple, satisfying, and full of flavor**

## Mercado el Cien

Even though it’s technically a pop-up market, this one is referred to as a mercado, and for good reason. It was the first major farmer’s market in Mexico City and has since become a go-to spot for locals and chefs searching for the freshest organic produce.

Its name comes from the concept that everything sold here is grown, raised, or produced within a 100-mile radius. That may not always hold true today, but it’s still one of the best places to connect directly with the people growing your food.

Showing up in your hippest outfit and carrying your trendiest tote isn’t required, but it’s definitely encouraged.

**This is also where I discovered (and instantly fell in love with) Simbiotica kombucha, so make sure to grab a bottle while you’re there.**

![Image 10](http://www.thecuriousmexican.com/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/Mercado_el_cien_2-1024x768.jpg)

**Whole Foods Market, Inc.** (colloquially referred to as simply **Whole Foods**) is an American multinational [supermarket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermarket "Supermarket")[chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chain_store "Chain store") headquartered in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas"), which generally sells [whole food](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_food "Whole food") products free from [hydrogenated fats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrogenated_fat "Hydrogenated fat") and [artificial colors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_colors "Artificial colors"), [flavors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_flavors "Artificial flavors"), and [preservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preservatives "Preservatives").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-7) A [USDA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USDA "USDA")[Certified Organic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Certified_Organic "Certified Organic") grocer in the United States, the chain is popularly known for its [organic selections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organic_food "Organic food").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-8)

[John Mackey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mackey_(businessman) "John Mackey (businessman)"), the last remaining co-founder of Whole Foods Market, sold the company to Amazon [for $13.7 billion on August 28, 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mergers_and_acquisitions_by_Amazon "List of mergers and acquisitions by Amazon").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-9)As of March 4,2019[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit), Whole Foods has more than 500 stores in North America and six in the United Kingdom.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-WholeFoodsCompanyInfo-5)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-locations-10)

### Early years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early years")]

In 1978, [John Mackey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mackey_(businessman) "John Mackey (businessman)") and Renee Lawson borrowed $45,000 from family and friends to open a small [vegetarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetarianism "Vegetarianism") natural foods store called SaferWay in [Austin, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin,_Texas "Austin, Texas") (the name being a [spoof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parody "Parody") of [Safeway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safeway_Inc. "Safeway Inc.")). When the two were evicted for storing food products in their apartment, they decided to live at the store. Because it was zoned for commercial use, there was no shower stall, so they bathed using a water hose attached to their dishwasher.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-marketplace-13)

Two years later, Mackey and Lawson partnered with Craig Weller and Mark Skiles to merge SaferWay with the latter's Clarksville Natural Grocery, resulting in the opening of the original Whole Foods Market, which included meat products. At 10,500 square feet (980 m 2) and with a staff of 19, the store was large in comparison to the standard [health food store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_food_store "Health food store") of the time.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-history-14)

On May 25, 1981, the most [damaging flood in 100 years](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoal_Creek,_Austin,_Texas#Flooding "Shoal Creek, Austin, Texas") devastated Austin. Whole Foods' inventory was ruined, and most of the equipment was damaged. The loss was approximately $400,000, and Whole Foods Market had no insurance. Customers, neighbors, and staff assisted in repairing and cleaning up the damage. Creditors, vendors, and investors assisted in the recovery, and the store reopened 28 days later.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-history-14)

### Expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Expansion")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4a/Whole_Foods_Market_in_the_Lower_East_Side_of_New_York.jpg/250px-Whole_Foods_Market_in_the_Lower_East_Side_of_New_York.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whole_Foods_Market_in_the_Lower_East_Side_of_New_York.jpg)

The Whole Foods Market on [Bowery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bowery "Bowery"), in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), is the largest grocery store in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-15)

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Bread_%26_circus_bakery_Medford_.jpg/250px-Bread_%26_circus_bakery_Medford_.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bread_&_circus_bakery_Medford_.jpg)

A Bread & Circus and Whole Foods bakery in [Medford, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medford,_Massachusetts "Medford, Massachusetts")

Beginning in 1984, Whole Foods Market expanded from Austin, first to [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston "Houston") and [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas") and then to New Orleans with the purchase of The Whole Food Co. in 1988. In 1989, the company expanded to the West Coast with a store in [Palo Alto, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California").

The company made its [initial public offering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering "Initial public offering") on January 23, 1992. The company's ticker symbol on the [Nasdaq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nasdaq "Nasdaq") was WFM.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-17)

While opening new stores, the company fueled rapid growth by acquiring other natural foods chains throughout the 1990s: Wellspring Grocery of [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), Bread & Circus of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") and [Rhode Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhode_Island "Rhode Island") (banner retired in 2003), Mrs. Gooch's Natural Foods Markets of Los Angeles,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-18) Bread of Life of Northern California, Fresh Fields Markets on the East Coast and in the Midwest, Bread of Life of Florida, Detroit-area Merchant of Vino stores, and Nature's Heartland of Boston.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-timeline-19) The company purchased Allegro Coffee Company in 1997.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-20) The company's 100th store was opened in [Torrance, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrance,_California "Torrance, California"), in 1999.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-21)

The company started its third decade with additional acquisitions. The first was Natural Abilities in 2000, which did business as Food for Thought in [Northern California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_California "Northern California").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-22) After the departure of then company president Chris Hitt and regional president Rich Cundiff, Southern California region, John Mackey promoted A. C. Gallo, president of the Northeast region, and [Walter Robb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Robb "Walter Robb"), president of the Northern California region to co-COO and soon after added the titles of co-president. This led to the promotion of three new regional presidents and a new era for the company. David Lannon became president of the Northeast region, Anthony Gilmore became president of the Southwest region, and Ron Megehan became the Northern California region, president. In 2001, Whole Foods also moved into [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-23) Later that year, [Ken Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Meyer "Ken Meyer") became president of the newly formed South region and Whole Foods Market acquired the assets of Harry's Farmers Market, which included three stores in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-24) In 2002, the company continued its expansion in North America and opened its first store in [Toronto, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-25) Further continuing its expansion, Select Fish of [Seattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle "Seattle") was acquired in 2003.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-26)

In late 2004, it was reported that Whole Foods had "cleared $188 million in profits in the last two years."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-27)

In 2005, Whole Foods opened its 80,000 sq ft (7,400 m 2) flagship store in [downtown Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtown_Austin "Downtown Austin"). The company's headquarters moved into offices above the store.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-28)

Whole Foods opened its first store in Hawaii in 2008[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-29) and in 2008 it also opened a southeast distribution center in [Braselton, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braselton,_Georgia "Braselton, Georgia"), calling it the first "green distribution center" for the company.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-30)

Along with new acquisitions, such as the 2014 purchase of seven [Dominick's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominick's "Dominick's") Finer Foods locations in Chicago, Whole Foods has also sold stores to other companies.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-31) For example, 35 Henry's Farmers Market and Sun Harvest Market stores were sold to a subsidiary of Los Angeles grocer [Smart & Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_&_Final "Smart & Final") Inc. for $166 million in 2007.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-32)

Whole Foods opened its second store in western New York in [Amherst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst,_New_York "Amherst, New York"), a suburb of [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York") in September 2017.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-35)

As part of a streamlining campaign, in January 2017, the company reported that it would close three remaining regional kitchens in [Everett, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everett,_Massachusetts "Everett, Massachusetts"); [Landover, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landover,_Maryland "Landover, Maryland"); and [Atlanta, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta,_Georgia "Atlanta, Georgia").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-reut1-36)

In June 2017, Amazon purchased Whole Foods Market for $13.7 billion.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-37) Amazon plans for Whole Foods customers who also have an [Amazon Prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime "Amazon Prime") account to be able to order groceries online and then pick them up in store for free.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-38)

In January 2019, to facilitate expansion into previously unserved areas, Amazon announced plans to acquire some former [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") and [Kmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kmart_(United_States) "Kmart (United States)") locations from [Sears Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears_Holdings "Sears Holdings"), which filed for [Chapter 11 Bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_11,_Title_11,_United_States_Code "Chapter 11, Title 11, United States Code") protection on October 15, 2018. These vacant locations would be demolished or remodeled to create new Whole Foods Market locations.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-40)

In April 2019, Whole Foods opened its largest store in the Southeast in Midtown Atlanta. The three-level store has a burger restaurant, an Allegro Coffee shop, and a rooftop terrace.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-41)

#### International expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: International expansion")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Whole_Foods_Market_Vancouver_Broadway_Store_Interior_2018.jpg/250px-Whole_Foods_Market_Vancouver_Broadway_Store_Interior_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Whole_Foods_Market_Vancouver_Broadway_Store_Interior_2018.jpg)

Whole Foods Market in [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"), British Columbia, Canada

Whole Foods entered the Canadian market in 2002 with a 40,000 sq ft (3,700 m 2) location in [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), at the upscale [Hazelton Lanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazelton_Lanes "Hazelton Lanes") shopping center in the city's [Yorkville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkville,_Toronto "Yorkville, Toronto") neighborhood.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-retail-insider-42) In 2013, with nine Whole Foods stores already running in Canada (all of them in Toronto and Vancouver area), the company's co-founder and CEO Mackey stated forecasts of opening 40 more stores in the country over an unspecified timeframe and eventually reaching $1-billion in annual Canadian sales.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-fpost-more-43) By January 2017—while announcing cancellation of 2015-2016 plans to open stores in [Calgary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calgary "Calgary") and [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton")—Whole Foods had 467 stores in three countries, majority of which were in the United States, except 9 in the United Kingdom and 12 in Canada.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-star-cancel-44) Among the twelve Canadian stores were five each in [Greater Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Vancouver "Greater Vancouver") and [Greater Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Toronto_Area "Greater Toronto Area"), and one each in [Ottawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottawa "Ottawa") and [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria,_British_Columbia "Victoria, British Columbia").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-star-cancel-44) In March 2020 there were 487 stores in the US, 14 in Canada and 7 in the UK.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-locations-10)

In 2004, Whole Foods Market entered the UK by acquiring seven Fresh & Wild stores.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-timeline-19)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-renton-45) In June 2007, it opened its first full-size store, a total of 80,000 sq ft (7,400 m 2) on three levels, on the site of the old [Barkers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barkers_of_Kensington "Barkers of Kensington") department store on [Kensington High Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensington_High_Street "Kensington High Street"), West London and currently their largest store in the world. Company executives claimed that as many as forty stores might eventually be opened throughout the UK.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-46) However, by September 2008, in the wake of Whole Foods Market's financial troubles, Fresh & Wild had been reduced to four stores, all in London. The flagship [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol") branch closed because it had "not met profitability goals."[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-47) In the year to September 28, 2008, the UK subsidiary lost £36 million due to a large [impairment charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impairment_charge "Impairment charge") of £27 million and poor trading results due to the growing fears of a global recession.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-48) However, in 2011, global sales grew +8% each financial quarter as shoppers returned to the chain.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-49) A first Scottish store was opened on November 16, 2011, in [Giffnock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giffnock "Giffnock"), Glasgow, which was closed in November 2017 along with the company's [Cheltenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheltenham "Cheltenham") store as part of a rationalization plan.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-51) Whole Foods Market Inc. currently operates five different Whole Foods locations, all in [Greater London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London "Greater London"): in [Camden Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camden_Town "Camden Town"), [Clapham Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapham_Junction_(area) "Clapham Junction (area)"), [Kensington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kensington "Kensington"), [Piccadilly Circus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piccadilly_Circus "Piccadilly Circus") and [Stoke Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoke_Newington "Stoke Newington").

#### Acquisition of Wild Oats Markets and antitrust complaint

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Acquisition of Wild Oats Markets and antitrust complaint")]

On February 21, 2007, Whole Foods Market, Inc. and [Wild Oats Markets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Oats_Markets "Wild Oats Markets") Inc. announced the signing of a merger agreement under which Whole Foods Market, Inc. would acquire Wild Oats Markets Inc.'s outstanding common stock in a cash tender offer of $18.50 per share, or approximately $565 million based on fully diluted shares. Under the agreement, Whole Foods Market, Inc. would also assume Wild Oats Markets Inc.'s net debt totaling approximately $106 million as reported on September 30, 2006.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-52)

On June 27, 2007, the [Federal Trade Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Trade_Commission "Federal Trade Commission") (FTC) issued an administrative complaint challenging Whole Foods Market, Inc.'s acquisition of Wild Oats Markets Inc. According to the complaint, the FTC believed that the proposed transaction would violate federal [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitrust "Antitrust") laws by eliminating the substantial competition between two close competitors in the operation of premium natural and organic supermarkets nationwide. The FTC contended that if the transaction were to proceed, Whole Foods Market would have the ability to raise prices and reduce quality and services. Both Whole Foods Market and Wild Oats stated their intention to oppose the FTC's complaint vigorously, and a court hearing on the issue was scheduled for July 31 and August 1, 2007. CEO John Mackey started a blog[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-53) on the subject to explain his opposition to the FTC's stance. Further blogging by Mackey was revealed when the FTC released papers detailing highly opinionated comments under the pseudonym "Rahodeb" that he made to the Whole Foods [Yahoo!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yahoo! "Yahoo!") investment message board. This became the subject of an investigation when the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") (SEC) noted that the Regulation Fair Disclosure law of 2000 may have been violated.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-55) The SEC cleared Mackey of the charges on April 25, 2008.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-56)

On July 29, 2008, the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia overturned the district court's decision to allow the merger. The Court of Appeals ruled that "premium natural, and organic supermarkets" ("PNOS"), such as Whole Foods and Wild Oats, constitute a distinct submarket of all grocers. The court ruled that "mission-driven" consumers (those with an emphasis on social and environmental responsibility) would be adversely affected by the merger because substantial evidence by the FTC showed that Whole Foods intended to raise prices after the consummation of the merger.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-57) As part of its effort to combat the ruling, Whole Foods subpoenaed financial records, market studies, and future strategic plans belonging to [New Seasons Market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Seasons_Market "New Seasons Market"), a regional competitor based in the Portland area.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-59) In 2009, Whole Foods agreed to sell the Wild Oats chain.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-60)

### 2017–present: Amazon subsidiary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2017–present: Amazon subsidiary")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Produce_section_of_a_Whole_Foods_Market_in_Crystal_City%2C_Virginia%2C_in_2019.jpg/250px-Produce_section_of_a_Whole_Foods_Market_in_Crystal_City%2C_Virginia%2C_in_2019.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Produce_section_of_a_Whole_Foods_Market_in_Crystal_City,_Virginia,_in_2019.jpg)

Interior of a Whole Foods Market in [Crystal City, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_City,_Virginia "Crystal City, Virginia"), in 2019, featuring Amazon branding

In February 2017, Whole Foods said it would close nine stores and lowered its financial projections for the year as the natural-foods company struggled with increased competition and slowing sales growth.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In late April 2017, Whole Foods reported their sixth consecutive quarter of declining sales and announced that the company would be closing nine stores: two each in Colorado and California, and one each in Georgia, Arizona, Utah, New Mexico, and Illinois. The loss of revenue was attributed to foot traffic being down and other supermarkets offering a similar experience for a lower cost.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-61)

In June 2017, [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") announced it would acquire Whole Foods Market,[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-ft-acquirew-63) adding some 400 physical stores to Amazon's e-commerce assets.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-ft-wall-64) The purchase was valued at $13.7 billion and caused Whole Foods's stock price to soar after the announcement was made.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-65)

In 2018, Whole Foods announced its possible intention to take over some vacant [Sears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears "Sears") and [Kmart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kmart_(United_States) "Kmart (United States)") stores and refurbish them after [Sears Holdings Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sears_Holdings_Corporation "Sears Holdings Corporation"), which owned both chains, filed for [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankruptcy "Bankruptcy") in October.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-66)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Amazon_One_-_Pay_With_Your_Palm_-_Verifone_Payment_Terminal_%2853816682453%29.jpg/250px-Amazon_One_-_Pay_With_Your_Palm_-_Verifone_Payment_Terminal_%2853816682453%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amazon_One_-_Pay_With_Your_Palm_-_Verifone_Payment_Terminal_(53816682453).jpg)

[Amazon One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_One "Amazon One") biometric payment system at a Whole Foods store in [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.")

In April 2022, Whole Foods in Austin, Texas, began allowing consumers to make purchases by scanning their palms. The system uses the [Amazon One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_One "Amazon One") system connected to a customer's debit or credit card.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-67)

In September 2022, [John Mackey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mackey_(businessman) "John Mackey (businessman)") stepped down from his position as [CEO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_executive_officer "Chief executive officer") of the company, one he held since its inception in 1980.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-68) Jason Buechel succeeded him. Buechel previously was executive vice president and [chief information officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_information_officer "Chief information officer") (CIO) between 2013 and 2019, followed by a tenure as [chief operating officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_operating_officer "Chief operating officer") (COO) from 2019 until his promotion in 2022.

In March 2024, Whole Foods announced they will close their Fulham and Richmond stores in the UK, as well as their distribution center in Dartford. The Amazon-owned supermarket also announced that they have signed a lease for a new store on King's Road in London's Chelsea, expected to open its doors in 2025.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-69)

In January 2025 workers at a Whole Foods Market in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") voted to become the first [unionized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_unions_in_the_United_States "Labor unions in the United States") store in the grocery chain,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-workers-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-union-71) hoping that a union could help negotiate higher [wages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wages "Wages") and better benefits.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-union-71) Whole Foods said it was "disappointed" by the unionization.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-fields-72) In February 2025, Whole Foods asked the [National Labor Relations Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Labor_Relations_Board "National Labor Relations Board") to reject the results of the union election, making unspecified allegations that the election was invalid.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-73)

## Product quality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Product quality")]

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/88/Wholefoodsmarket_caryproduce.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wholefoodsmarket_caryproduce.jpg)

Produce in a [Cary, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cary,_North_Carolina "Cary, North Carolina"), store

Whole Foods Market sells only products that meet its internally developed, proprietary quality standards for being "natural," which the store defines as minimally processed foods that are free of hydrogenated fats as well as [artificial flavors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_flavoring "Artificial flavoring"), [colors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_coloring "Food coloring"), [sweeteners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_substitutes "Sugar substitutes"), [preservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preservatives "Preservatives"), and many others as listed on their online "Unacceptable Food Ingredients" list.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-quality_standards-74) Whole Foods also stated its intent not to sell meat or milk from [cloned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloning "Cloning") animals or their offspring, even though the U.S. [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration") (FDA) has ruled them safe to eat.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-75)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-clone-76)

The company also sells many USDA-certified organic foods and products that aim to be environmentally friendly and ecologically responsible. Stores do not carry [foie gras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foie_gras "Foie gras") or eggs from hens confined to [battery cages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_cages "Battery cages") due to animal cruelty concerns as a result of successful advocacy by animal welfare groups. The Whole Foods website details the company's criteria for selling food, dietary supplements, and personal care products.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-quality_standards-74)

Until June 2011, body care products sold at Whole Foods could be marketed as organic even if they contained ingredients not listed by the USDA as acceptable for use in organic food.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-Organic_Body_Care_Policy-77) "Products made using petroleum-derived and other synthetic or chemical ingredients, prohibited in organic foods, can be found among the organic shampoos and lotions made by Avalon, Nature's Gate, Jason Natural Cosmetics, Kiss My Face and other brands," said Urvashi Rangan, an environmental health scientist at [Consumer Reports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_Reports "Consumer Reports"). This is because the federal guidelines that regulate organic food labeling do not apply to cosmetics.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-78) Starting in June 2011, personal care products sold at Whole Foods Market were required to follow the same USDA National Organic Program standards for organic food. This required products labeled "Organic" to contain 95 percent or more certified organic ingredients.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-Organic_Body_Care_Policy-77)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d2/Parmesan_Cheese_Wheel_-_Whole_Foods.JPG/250px-Parmesan_Cheese_Wheel_-_Whole_Foods.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Parmesan_Cheese_Wheel_-_Whole_Foods.JPG)

Opening a wheel of [Parmigiano-Reggiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parmigiano-Reggiano "Parmigiano-Reggiano") cheese at Whole Foods Market in [Overland Park, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overland_Park,_Kansas "Overland Park, Kansas")

In a _[Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall\_Street\_Journal "Wall Street Journal")_ article in August 2009, John Mackey acknowledged that his company had lost touch with its natural food roots and would attempt to reconnect with the idea that health was affected by the quality of food consumed. He said, "We sell a bunch of junk." He stated that the company would focus more on health education in its stores.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-79) As of 2013, many stores have employed Healthy Eating Specialists who are team members who "answer customers' healthy eating questions and can assist ... in choosing the most nutrient-dense ingredients, suggest satisfying healthy recipes," and help "create a meal plan in keeping with your health goals."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-80)

In early April 2025, the bakery, deli, and cooked foods sections of Whole Foods in [Cupertino, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cupertino,_California "Cupertino, California"), were closed down by local health authorities due to repeated violations and failure to remediate the presence of rodents and rodent droppings.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-81)

## Rating systems

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Rating systems")]

Whole Foods Market has developed several in-store rating systems for various departments to allow their customers full transparency in purchasing. The Seafood department has a Sustainability Rating System for wild-caught seafood[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-82) while farm-raised seafood has to meet aquaculture standards[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-83) both rated in accordance to third-party auditors. The Meat department has a rating system in partnership with the Global Animal Partnership based on animal welfare.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-84) The produce department has a rating system based on farming practices which include measures of a farm's environment, GMO transparency, worker safety, and wage practices.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-85) The grocery department has an Eco-scale rating system for its cleaning products which measures their environmental impact.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-86) Each system is in place to allow customers to make the most educated choices within Whole Foods Market. There are efforts to create more rating systems in other departments.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-87)

## GMO product labeling

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: GMO product labeling")]

Whole Foods Market has announced plans to provide its customers GMO ([genetically modified organism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetically_modified_organism "Genetically modified organism")) product labeling by 2018.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-wholefoodsmarket.com-88) Efforts of GMO transparency run the gamut of each department. For years, Non-GMO Project Verified items have been sought in Grocery.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-wholefoodsmarket.com-88) While efforts continue in Produce, Whole Foods recommends buying organic or referring to their "Responsibly Grown produce rating system [which] requires growers to disclose the use of GMO seeds or plant material."[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-wholefoodsmarket.com-88) In Seafood, plans are being made to launch a Non-GMO Project Verification process for farm-raised fish.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-wholefoodsmarket.com-88) Currently, there are no USDA Organic regulations for farmed seafood.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-89)

## Purchasing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Purchasing")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Beer_at_a_grocery_store_in_New_York_City.JPG/250px-Beer_at_a_grocery_store_in_New_York_City.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beer_at_a_grocery_store_in_New_York_City.JPG)

Whole Foods Market has opened wine and beer shops to cater to their upmarket brand. Above, the imported beer case at a Whole Foods beer shop.

Whole Foods Market purchases products for retail sale from local, regional, and international wholesale suppliers and vendors. Most purchasing occurs at the regional and national levels to negotiate volume discounts with major vendors and distributors. Regional and store buyers focus on local products and any unique products necessary to ensure a neighborhood market feel. Whole Foods says that the company is committed to buying from local producers that meet its quality standards while also increasingly focusing more of its purchasing on producer- and manufacture-direct programs.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-90) Some regions have an employee known as a "forager," whose sole duty is to source local products for each store.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-91)

### Whole Trade Guarantee

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Whole Trade Guarantee")]

In April 2007, Whole Foods Market launched the Whole Trade Guarantee, a purchasing initiative emphasizing ethics and social responsibility concerning products imported from the developing world. The criteria include fair prices for crops, environmentally sound practices, better wages and labor conditions for workers, and the stipulation that one percent of proceeds from Whole Trade-certified products go to the Whole Planet Foundation to support micro-loan programs in developing countries. The company's goal, published in 2007, is to have at least half of its imported products from these countries fully certified by 2017.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-93)

## Efforts

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Whole_Foods_Market&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Efforts")]

Whole Foods Market has a policy of donating at least five percent of its annual net profits to charitable causes. Some of this mandate is accomplished through store-level donations held on certain "5% days" throughout the year. The rest of it comes from various targeted projects by the company.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whole_Foods_Market#cite_note-94)

### Environmental involvement
